figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 1. A brief overview of the sources, applications, and synthesis methods of paclitaxel. Paclitaxel is derived from plants of the genus Taxus and is primarily used in 
the treatment of cancer. Its production methods mainly include total chemical synthesis, semi-synthetic methods, heterologous cultivation in plant systems, pro­
duction by endophytic fungi of the genus Taxus, and heterologous cultivation in microbial systems.

Fig. 3. Schematic diagram of the three-dimensional structure of TXS, catalytic pocket, metal-binding motifs, and catalytic mechanism. (A) The structure of TXS 
consists of three α-helix bundle domains (α, β, γ), featuring structural characteristics of Class I (α) and Class II (β and γ) cyclases, but retaining only the active motifs 
required for Class I cyclases, forming an active pocket at its C-terminus that can bind and catalyze the substrate. (B) In the catalytic active pocket of TXS, three 
magnesium ions interact with the conserved metal-binding motifs D613DMAD617 and N757DTKT761YQAE765. All molecules in the structure diagram are shown as stick 
models. Gray spheres represent magnesium ions; blue regions represent metal-binding motifs; yellow regions represent substrate analogs. (C) The specific process by 
which TXS facilitates cyclization.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 4
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 4. Schematic diagram of the phylogenetic trees of CYP450s present in Taxus and the motifs prediction of CYP450s involved in hydroxylation within the 
paclitaxel biosynthetic pathway. (A) Phylogenic analysis of A-type and non-A-type CYP450 families. The green and orange branches represent the sequences from 
Arabidopsis and T. chinensis var. mairei, respectively. The dots denote CYP450 genes, while the outermost circle represents the CYP450 gene family. Reprinted with 
permission from Ref. [12]. Copyright 2025 Springer Nature. (B) Prediction of conserved motifs for seven CYP450s involved in the hydroxylation process of paclitaxel 
biosynthesis.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 5
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 5. Schematic diagram of the three-dimensional structure of CYP725A4, the positioning of taxadiene and heme, the key amino acids related to substrate binding, 
and the reaction mechanism by which CYP725A4 catalyzes the conversion of taxadiene to T5OH. (A) Three-dimensional structure of CYP725A4. (B) The crystal 
structure of CYP725A4 shows that the substrate taxadiene is positioned above the heme molecule, with its C5 and C20 atoms located close to the heme iron at 
distances of 4.3 Å and 3.8 Å, respectively. (C) The stability of the substrate primarily depends on hydrophobic interactions with surrounding residues. The residues 
M123, W125, F129, M133, L225, F229, and H305 are critical residues surrounding the substrate and are essential for the catalytic function of CYP725A4. The 
residues S302, L303, T310, P373, V374, and P484 do not directly participate in substrate binding. (D) Two catalytic mechanisms of CYP725A4 for the conversion of 
taxadiene/iso-taxadiene to T5OH. (B)-(D), reprinted (adapted) with permission from Ref. [72]. Copyright 2025 American Chemical Society.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 6
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 6. Schematic diagram of the acylation reactions of BAHD acyltransferase family, phylogenetic analysis of Taxus BAHD acyltransferases, and the motif prediction 
of ACTs involved in hydroxylation within the paclitaxel biosynthetic pathway. (A) Acylation reactions of the BAHD acyltransferases. (B) The tree is generated using 
the neighbor-joining method. The pink-red circle represents the transferase genes in T. chinensis var. mairei. All identified BAHD acyltransferase genes involved in the 
paclitaxel pathway are classified in Group 1 of Clade V. Reprinted with permission from Ref. [12]. Copyright 2025 Springer Nature. (C) Prediction of conserved 
motifs for five ACTs involved in the acylation process of the paclitaxel biosynthetic pathway.

figure_candidates.label: Figure 7
figure_candidates.caption:
Fig. 7. Schematic diagram of AI-assisted protein engineering and metabolic engineering. In AI-driven iterative protein design for paclitaxel biosynthesis, workflows 
start with curating enzyme sequence, structure, and functional data to train machine learning models. These models then predict promising mutations and guide the 
generation of a focused mutant library. Finally, laboratory screening of this library validates mutant activity and feeds data back to refine model predictions, 
accelerating optimal enzyme identification. Computational metabolic design utilizes genome-scale metabolic network models for computational analysis, enabling 
the automated synchronized evolution of multiple key genes in metabolic pathways. The resulting optimal experimental scheme is then validated in the laboratory to 
observe whether there is a significant increase in the yield of the target product.
